title: A wedding song at a funeral
hook: Sohila is also sung at cremations, a song of the soul going home

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was what did I earn today. It's a week's end too: the sky's aarti, the wind, the city of thieves, Guru Arjan's request. Today, where else Sohila is sung.
screen: `WHAT DID I EARN TODAY.` · `A WEEK: THE AARTI, THE CITY, THE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: A first-dance song at a graveside would stop a room cold. Yet at a Sikh cremation, once the fire is lit, the words recited sound, to anyone who knows them, like a wedding: the date written, oil poured at the threshold, friends asked for their blessings, a bride called to meet her Lord. It's Sohila, the same five hymns said at bedtime. Here the wedding words aren't a mistake. They're the point.
screen: `WEDDING MUSIC, FUNERAL MUSIC.` → `AT THE CREMATION: SOHILA.` → `THE SAME FIVE HYMNS AS LAST NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, sets out the funeral. The body is washed and dressed, and the family gathers. At the cremation ground, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila, and then the Ardas is said. In the days that follow, a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib is begun, at home or at a gurdwara. Sikh teaching also asks mourners not to give way to loud wailing. Grief is real, and tears are human, but the songs are of praise. So why Sohila? Go back to its first hymn. The date has been written. Friends, pour the oil, give your blessings, so I may meet my Lord. The summons goes to every house, every day. Read at the pyre, the funeral becomes the day that summons arrives for one soul, and the wedding is the meeting with the Beloved. In the hymn's language, the person who has died isn't lost to darkness. They're going home, the way a bride goes to her new home. And if the same five hymns are sung at bedtime and at the end of a life, some readers hear every night as a small rehearsal: lying down, letting go of the day, trusting the morning to the One. The last line of Sohila, sung at the pyre as at the pillow, is Guru Arjan asking to be the dust of the holy's feet. Even at the end, humility.
screen: `THE PYRE IS LIT; SOHILA IS SUNG.` · `PRAISE INSTEAD OF WAILING.` · `THE SUMMONS ARRIVES FOR ONE SOUL.` · `EVERY NIGHT, A SMALL REHEARSAL.` · then, large: `GOING HOME.`

segments.voice: Let one person who has died come to mind, a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, and picture their face on a good day, with one kindness, one habit, one laugh of theirs. If grief comes, let it come; nothing needs fixing. Hold them like a friend at the door wishing a traveler well, and if you pray, say Waheguru for them, softly.
Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct that sets out the funeral: Kirtan Sohila is sung there as well as at bedtime, the soul as a bride, called to meet the Beloved and going home.
Your line: going home. Praise and trust, at the end of a day and of a life. Day four hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: At a Sikh cremation, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila and then the Ardas, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada directs; the same hymns are said by Sikhs every night before sleep.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's strange to sing about a wedding at a funeral.

what a scholar hears: the Sikh Rehat Maryada prescribes Kirtan Sohila and Ardas at the cremation, and discourages wailing; the first hymn itself calls what it sings a sohila, a song of praise.

chat.says: Why would a Sikh funeral use a hymn full of wedding images?
options: In Sohila the soul is the bride, the wedding is meeting God; it fits a soul going home.
It's a mix-up; a wedding hymn was put into the funeral by mistake long ago.
It's sung to cheer mourners up, so nobody has to think about the death.
chat.meaning: The Rehat Maryada has Kirtan Sohila recited at the pyre; in its first hymn the soul is a bride called to meet the Beloved.

notes: Rehat Maryada funeral order: Kirtan Sohila recited when the pyre is fully lit, followed by Ardas; a sahaj or akhand path afterward is common; mourners asked not to wail. Confirm details and wording.
Review replaced the trapdoor's 'sohila was also a name for festive songs' with the first hymn's own use of the word (tit ghar gaavahu sohila). Confirm.
